prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- The woman and children held captive in a cellar for years by their incestuous father will take years to recover from their disturbing ordeal, doctors warned Wednesday as the family at the center of the case remained in psychiatric care. The bathroom used by Elizabeth Fritzl, who was held captive for more than two decades, and her three children. Members of the Fritzl family will also be offered the chance to adopt new identities in an effort to help them lead normal lives, officials said. Hans-Heinz Lenze, the head of local social services said the family was "doing as well as can be expected in the circumstances" and said any change of identity would be the family's decision. Elizabeth Fritzl -- now 42 -- spent more than two decades in the windowless basement after being drugged, handcuffed and locked up by her father, Josef Fritzl, as an 18-year-old. Repeatedly raped, she gave birth to seven children by Fritzl, one of whom died as an infant. Three of the children -- Kerstin, 19; Stefan, 18; and Felix, 5 -- remained imprisoned underground with their mother. The other three lived in an apartment upstairs with Fritzl and his wife who believed Elizabeth had abandoned them after running away from home. Elizabeth and five of the children were continuing to receive treatment at a local clinic near Amstetten after being reunited on Sunday. Kerstin, whose hospitalization at the weekend finally brought the family's plight to the attention of authorities, remained in a coma at a nearby hospital. "It is astonishing how easy it worked that the children came together, and also it was astonishing how easy it happened that the grandmother and the mother came together," clinic director Berthold Kepplinger said. But Kepplinger warned that the family would require extensive counseling. "We're talking of 20 years of darkness, incest and its effects and other illnesses they might have suffered from." Kepplinger said the two sets of children were tentatively getting to know one another, adding that the two boys who had lived underground had an unusual way of communicating with each other. A policeman who had accompanied the boys to hospital after their discovery on Sunday said the pair had "screamed with excitement" during the car journey as they experienced the outside world for the first time. "The two boys appeared overawed by the daylight they had never experienced before," said Chief Inspector Leopold Etz. "The real world was completely alien to them... We had to drive very slowly with them because they cringed at every car light and every bump. It was as if we had just landed on the moon." In an interview with the Austrian newspaper, Oesterreich, psychiatrist Max Friedrich, who treated the abducted teenager Natascha Kampusch, estimated it would take "between five and eight years" for the children to recover from their experiences. Another psychologist, Bernd Prosser, told Austrian television that it would be impossible for the four held prisoner underground to lead normal lives. "I am afraid it is too late for that." Kampusch, the Austrian girl abducted as a 10-year-old and held captive in a basement for more than eight years until she escaped in 2007, also offered her help to the family on Tuesday, but questioned the decision to move them from the cellar into psychiatric care. "Pulling them abruptly out of this situation, without transition, to hold them and isolating them to some extent, it can't be good for them," said Kampusch, now 20, in an interview with Austrian TV station Puls 4. "I believe it might have been even better to leave them where they were, but that was probably impossible. This case is not like mine, where that was not my environment. They were born there and I can imagine that there is a strong attachment to that place." E-mail to a friend .

(CNN) — Doctors said Wednesday that the woman and children confined for years in a basement by her father, who sexually abused her, could need years to recover from the trauma. Meanwhile, members of the family remained under psychiatric care.

The cellar included a bathroom used by Elisabeth Fritzl and the three children who were imprisoned with her during her captivity of more than 20 years.

Officials said the Fritzl family could also choose to assume new identities to help them build more normal lives. Hans-Heinz Lenze, who headed local social services, said they were coping “as well as can be expected in the circumstances,” adding that the decision to change identities would be theirs.

Elisabeth Fritzl, then 42, was 18 when her father, Josef Fritzl, drugged her, put her in handcuffs and locked her inside a windowless basement. During more than two decades of confinement and repeated rape, she gave birth to seven children fathered by Fritzl. One died in infancy.

Three children—Kerstin, 19; Stefan, 18; and Felix, 5—were kept underground with Elisabeth. Three others were raised in the apartment above by Fritzl and his wife, who believed Elisabeth had run away and abandoned the children.

After the family members were reunited Sunday, Elisabeth and five of the children continued receiving care at a clinic near Amstetten. Kerstin, whose admission to a hospital over the weekend led authorities to discover the family’s circumstances, remained comatose at another nearby hospital.

Clinic director Berthold Kepplinger said it was remarkable how readily the two groups of children came together and how easily the grandmother and mother reunited. However, he cautioned that the family would need prolonged therapy, given “20 years of darkness,” incest, its consequences and any other medical problems they may have developed.

According to Kepplinger, the children raised upstairs and those held below ground were cautiously beginning to become acquainted. He also noted that the two boys who had lived in the basement communicated with each other in an unusual manner.

A police officer who traveled with the boys to the hospital after they were found Sunday said they “screamed with excitement” in the car while encountering the world outside for the first time.

Chief Inspector Leopold Etz said the boys seemed overwhelmed by daylight, something they had never previously experienced. The outside world was entirely unfamiliar to them, he said, and officers had to drive slowly because every vehicle light and bump made them recoil. Etz compared the experience to having just arrived on the moon.

Speaking to the Austrian newspaper *Oesterreich*, psychiatrist Max Friedrich—who had treated kidnapped teenager Natascha Kampusch—estimated that the children’s recovery would take “between five and eight years.”

Psychologist Bernd Prosser offered a more pessimistic assessment on Austrian television, saying the four people confined underground would never be able to live normally. “I am afraid it is too late for that,” he said.

Kampusch also offered assistance to the family Tuesday, while raising concerns about transferring them directly from the basement into psychiatric treatment. Kampusch was abducted in Austria at age 10 and held in a cellar for more than eight years before escaping in 2007.

In an interview with Austrian broadcaster Puls 4, Kampusch, then 20, argued that suddenly removing the family from their familiar surroundings, confining them elsewhere and keeping them somewhat isolated might not be beneficial. She suggested it could possibly have been better to leave them temporarily where they had lived, though she acknowledged that this was probably not feasible.

Kampusch emphasized that their case differed from hers: the place where she was imprisoned was never her home, while the children in the Fritzl case had been born in the basement and might therefore have developed a powerful emotional connection to it.

**Amstetten, Austria — May 2008**

In the weeks after Austrian police uncovered the crimes of Josef Fritzl, doctors placed his daughter Elisabeth and her surviving children together in a secure psychiatric-clinic complex near Amstetten. Elisabeth, then 42, had been imprisoned by her father for 24 years in a concealed cellar beneath the family home and repeatedly raped. She gave birth there to seven children; one infant died shortly after birth. Three children remained underground with her, while three others were taken upstairs and raised by Fritzl and his wife, Rosemarie, after he falsely claimed Elisabeth had abandoned them.

### Treatment and family reunification

The six surviving children—aged between five and 19—had grown up as two separate groups and initially had to become acquainted as siblings. Contemporary reports said the clinic gave the family private living quarters and round-the-clock protection from the press. A multidisciplinary team of psychiatrists, psychologists, pediatricians, nurses, social workers, and educational specialists supervised their care.

Treatment was deliberately gradual. Medical staff emphasized routine, privacy, and the family’s control over daily decisions after years in which Elisabeth had been denied all autonomy. The children received medical examinations, nutritional support, psychological counseling, schooling, and help adjusting to ordinary social life. Staff reportedly used games, art, and simple shared activities to help the siblings bond.

Kerstin, the eldest cellar-born child, was critically ill when the case came to light and initially remained in intensive care. Her collapse had prompted Fritzl to take her to hospital, setting in motion the investigation. She later regained consciousness and was eventually reunited with the rest of the family.

### First experiences outside the cellar

The three children raised underground—Kerstin, Stefan, and Felix—had lived without natural daylight, open space, changing weather, or ordinary contact with society. Early exposure to the outside world was therefore carefully controlled.

Reports described them being introduced slowly to daylight and fresh air, first through opened curtains and windows and later during short, protected outings on the clinic grounds. Everyday features of the natural world—sunlight, grass, trees, wind, rain, and the breadth of the sky—were unfamiliar and potentially overwhelming. Their eyes and skin needed time to adjust to sunlight, while their movement and posture had been affected by years in cramped rooms with low ceilings.

The youngest, Felix, was reported to be particularly curious and adaptable, although specialists cautioned that apparent excitement did not mean he was unaffected by trauma. Stefan, who had spent his entire childhood below ground, reportedly had difficulty walking fully upright because of the cellar’s restricted height. The older cellar-born children also faced the enormous task of learning social conventions and coping with an environment full of unfamiliar sounds, people, and choices.

### Prospects for recovery

Doctors repeatedly warned against predicting a quick or complete recovery. Contemporary estimates ranged from several years to a decade or more of intensive support. Some trauma specialists suggested that meaningful stabilization could take **five to eight years**, while others said the psychological effects would probably remain throughout the victims’ lives.

Clinicians stressed that “recovery” would not mean erasing the experience. The goals were safety, independence, education, family attachment, and the ability to live without constant domination by the trauma. The children’s ages and experiences differed sharply, so each required an individual plan. The three raised upstairs had also suffered profound harm: they had grown up within Fritzl’s control, had been deceived about their mother, and then learned the truth about their family.

Authorities withheld many details to protect the victims. Later reporting indicated that Elisabeth and the children adopted new identities and continued treatment in an undisclosed location. Medical officials said their privacy—not public curiosity—was essential to any chance of building stable lives.
